transcript: So let me set the scene. You may remember that we had decades, of course, of discrimination against African-Americans on housing. It was written into the law. The federal government subsidized housing for white people, discriminated against black people with red lining, and created this huge black white wealth gap. Laws changed in the mid-1960s. And you see that start to shrink. We actually prohibit that kind of discrimination. And you see, interestingly enough, white families housing goes up a little, and black families a lot more. So the gap is starting to close. And then, giant financial institutions turn around and see, whoa, there is big money now in housing in communities of color. So that's when they decide to start rolling out their predatory mortgages. I mean, the worst of the worst. And remember, this was not to help people buy homes. This was to come in and get people already owned homes to refinance and then lose their homes two years or four years later. So by the 2000s, I was ringing every alarm bell I could to say, no, no, no, this is terrible. This is a crisis coming our way. It's in communities of color. Look at the numbers on this and starting to spread across the country. And of course, ultimately that's what happened. And it brought down the entire economy in 2008. So my view of this was, look, it can't stop every form of corporate cheating in one bite. But you can at least make sure that they don't cheat in this way next time. And that is both targeting communities of color and cheating people on financial instruments, on home mortgages, credit cards, payday loans, all of these financial products. And so I started pushing for a consumer financial protection bureau. And the basic idea was pretty simple. a cop on the beat who would actually watch out for consumers. Pretty shocking idea, right? And specifically would have an office of discrimination. So it would look at discrimination and lending, which drains more and more money out of communities of color, targets people of color. So people started out telling me, you'll never get that passed. Don't even try. The big banks will never go along, the Republicans will never go, shoot a bunch of the Democrats will never go along with this. And so the way I heard this was try harder. And I just thought, I'm not going to let this moment pass without getting deep in this fight. So I proposed this agency, kept getting out there banging the drum for it. My colleague, President Obama, talked about it on late night TV. More and more folks got engaged. More groups came in. We had no natural constituency. It's not like there's some consumer groups specifically focused on that. And so during the course of the adoption of Dodd-Frank, this was my one thing I kept hammering on. And President Obama defended it from the White House even in some cases against people in his own administration and certainly against the big banks. By the way, the big banks during that period of time are estimated to have spent about a million dollars a day for over a year lobbying against that agency and against the financial reforms generally. Finally, we got enough outside pressure and with inside leadership with the president got it passed into law. And now that agency has forced giant financial institutions to return more than $12 billion directly to people that they cheated and has been an effective watchdog in beating back lending discrimination. During the Trump administration, that's kind of gone on to hold. They've had some terrible people in charge, but it makes a difference.
